In summary, our research is concerned with
the origin, distribution, and history of sedimentary rocks deposited in a stable, nonvolcanic, nonmarine environment.
the origin and history, as well as the stratigraphic and structural relations, of these formations.
the stratigraphy and sedimentology of the nonmarine rocks of the northern Bighhorn Basin and their relationships to the marine rocks of the Western Interior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Morrison, Cloverly and Sykes Mountain formational rocks are the products of a long period of nonmarine sedimentation in an area which was stable and free of volcanic eruptions.

these formations are the result of deposition of volcanic ash in lakes and swamps, of reworked volcanic debris in rivers and lakes, of reworked sedimentary and metamorphic detritus in rivers, and of shallow marine deposits.
the Morrison-Cloverly-Sykes Mountain sequence of rocks is a record of the slow accumulation of sediment in a stable depositional environment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the nonmarine sediments of the northern Bighhorn Basin are the product of an arid to semiarid, low-relief, tectonically stable, continental environment in which volcanic ash was a major source of detrital material.

the Bighorn and Wind River basins were a broad and shallow depression in the Late Jurassic, which was filled by the Sundance, Morrison, Cloverly and Sykes Mountain sediments and by volcanic debris, and which became the Bighorn basin during Early Cretaceous time.
the nonmarine rocks of the Bighorns were deposited under relatively stable, nonorogenic conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Bighorn basin was a stable area in the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous.
